newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Newsprint costs easing at Midland.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Newsprint costs easing at Midland.

text.p: Midland Independent Newspapers said on Wednesday that it had negotiated cuts of around 10 percent in its newsprint bill after a sharp rise hit its first half performance.

"We have experienced some reduction...They (newsprint costs) have come down to around the same level as this time last year," Finance Director John Whitehouse said in a telephone interview. He said the reduction had been in the order of 10 percent.
A rise of 2.3 million stg in newsprint costs was one of the factors behind a first half decline in pre-tax, pre-exceptional profit to 8.3 million stg from 9.4 million 12 months ago.
Midland's first half was also depressed by patchy advertising revenue caused by uncertain consumer demand.
Whitehouse said that the pre-Christmas period was a vital one for advertising revenue but it was not yet clear whether the situation would improve.
"October and November are key months but it's difficult to predict how things will go. We've not yet experienced any significant movement from the first-half trend," he said.
Whitehouse noted that the first-half result was above the minimum of 7.9 million stg referred to in a trading statement in early June.
That warning sent Midland shares crashing 19p to 128p, a level from which they are yet to make any real recovery. The shares added 1/2p to 130p on Wednesday.

Midland incurred exceptional costs of 1.4 million stg in the first half relating to an abortive acquisition. This is believed to refer to the sale of EMAP's regional newspapers, bought by Johnston Press for 211 million stg.
Other exceptional items were closure costs of 600,000 stg and a resulting balance sheet write-off of 2.6 million stg.
Midland said in a statement it would continue to consider acquistions in and outside its central England stronghold.
Whitehouse said that Midland was not interested in the 47 titles in southern England and south Wales which United News & Media is selling.
Midland has four main paid-for titles -- three in Britain's second city Birmingham and one in nearby Coventry. It also has around 40 freesheets.
Some media watchers have said that Midland could itself be a takeover target for ITV company Carlton. Carlton operates in the Midlands through its Central Television unit.
Midland is involved in cable television through Birmingham LIVE, a joint venture with Mirror Group.
